title: When the Letter Burns Again
premise: Insurance investigator Rosalind Yarrow is hired by a nervous stranger, prepaid in cash, to prove that a murder will not happen — the murder of a woman named Ada Fenwick, who has been dead for thirty years. As Rosalind digs into the town's founding families, she discovers her own photographic memory has been quietly edited: a night in 1994 that everyone remembers differently, including her. The client turns out to be Ada's son, returned to expose how his mother's death was disguised as an accident and paid off through the very insurance files Rosalind keeps. In the end, Rosalind must choose between preserving the town's fragile peace and burning the ledger of secrets — including her father's name on the payout — to finally let Ada rest.
about_author: Beatrix Zhou is the pen name of a former claims adjuster who spent a decade reading other people's disasters for a living before turning them into fiction. She writes from a coastal town much like Millbrook, where she insists every neighbor is fictional.

chapters.title: Paid in Advance
chapters.summary: Rosalind Yarrow's POV. A gray-eyed stranger named Corin Fenwick walks into her office and pays three months' retainer to prove a murder won't happen — naming his own mother, dead since 1994. Rosalind, who never forgets anything, is unsettled that his face triggers nothing. Emotional beat: professional curiosity curdling into unease.

chapters.title: The Alphabet of Small Crimes
chapters.summary: Rosalind surveys her filing system of the town's quiet scandals — affairs, forged checks, one drowning ruled accidental. Establishes her role as keeper of Millbrook's secrets and her rule against opening old files. Beat: controlled order masking loneliness.

chapters.title: Ada Fenwick, Deceased, Twice
chapters.summary: Rosalind pulls the 1994 file: Ada drowned at the quarry, ruled accidental, insurance paid to her husband Gerald. But the death certificate date and the policy payout date differ by nine days. POV alternates to Corin recalling his childhood. Beat: first crack in the official story.

chapters.title: Nine Days
chapters.summary: Rosalind interviews the retired coroner, who insists he signed the certificate on time — then can't find his copy. Someone has been sanitizing records recently, not thirty years ago. Beat: dread; the past is being actively rewritten now.

chapters.title: What the Water Kept
chapters.summary: Rosalind visits the quarry at dusk and finds fresh tire tracks and a burned patch where papers were torched. A scrap survives: part of a letter bearing Ada's handwriting — dated after her death. Beat: the title's promise lands; the letter burns again.

chapters.title: Gerald's Perfect Grief
chapters.summary: POV shift to Gerald Fenwick, respected patriarch, hosting the town's anniversary gala preparations. He recognizes Rosalind's surname and warns her gently off 'old water.' Beat: menace wrapped in courtesy.

chapters.title: Memory Is a Liar With Good Records
chapters.summary: Rosalind interrogates her own photographic memory of 1994 — she was fourteen, saw something at the quarry she has never examined. She realizes memory without scrutiny is just another archive no one audits. Beat: self-doubt; her gift becomes suspect.

chapters.title: The Widow's Club
chapters.summary: Three elderly women who knew Ada give Rosalind tea and contradictions: Ada was planning to leave Gerald; Ada would never leave her son; Ada couldn't swim but loved the water. One slips a photograph into Rosalind's coat. Beat: warmth laced with fear.

chapters.title: Correspondence From a Dead Woman
chapters.summary: The photograph shows Ada posting letters the week she died. Rosalind traces the addressee: a solicitor in the next county who kept copies per agreement. The letters allege Gerald's business fraud — motive. Beat: momentum; the case gains a spine.

chapters.title: Someone Follows the Investigator
chapters.summary: Rosalind notices a car tailing her, loses it, and finds her office lock scratched. Her files have been browsed, not taken — someone checking what she knows. Beat: paranoia; the hunter is hunted.

chapters.title: Corin's Alibi
chapters.summary: Corin admits he arrived in town two weeks ago under a false name and has been asking questions that got the coroner frightened. Rosalind must decide if he's avenger or manipulator. Beat: alliance tested; trust as evidence.

chapters.title: The Second Letter Burns
chapters.summary: A fire at the historical society destroys the 1994 donation box — including Ada's letters. Rosalind arrives too late but photographs the arsonist's silhouette; her memory holds what the camera missed. Beat: fury; escalation from erasure to violence.

chapters.title: My Father's Signature
chapters.summary: Rosalind finds the 1994 payout authorization in her late father's handwriting — he processed the claim, possibly falsified the dates. Her belonging to Millbrook was purchased with this silence. Beat: devastating midpoint reversal.

chapters.title: Thirteen Days of Silence
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, young Rosalind's POV, 1994: she saw her father come home soaked to the knees the night Ada died, and chose to forget. Beat: the price of survival made personal and irreversible.

chapters.title: The Man Who Wasn't There
chapters.summary: Present day: the tailing car belongs to a private investigator hired by Gerald — or so he claims, until Rosalind proves his retainer predates Corin's arrival. Gerald expected trouble before Corin ever came home. Beat: the net tightens around the true architect.

chapters.title: Confession at the Gala
chapters.summary: At the town's founding gala, Gerald publicly toasts Rosalind's father while privately offering her money and a warning. She accepts neither, and the widow's club watches from across the room. Beat: open war declared beneath civility.

chapters.title: What Ada Wrote Last
chapters.summary: The solicitor produces Ada's final letter, mailed the day she died: she feared Gerald, named a witness, and asked that the truth be published only if her son came looking. Corin reads his mother's voice for the first time in thirty years. Beat: grief and resolve fused.

chapters.title: The Witness Who Forgot on Purpose
chapters.summary: The named witness is Rosalind's father's old partner, now dying, who confesses he helped stage the accident and watched Rosalind's father take the fall for the paperwork. Beat: guilt distributed; no clean hands in Millbrook.

chapters.title: Quarry, Night, Third Time
chapters.summary: Climax. Gerald lures Rosalind and Corin to the quarry to retrieve 'the last letter,' intending a second staged drowning. Rosalind's total recall of the terrain, the widow's club arriving unbidden, and a recorded confession turn the trap shut. Beat: terror, then reversal.

chapters.title: Arithmetic of a Life
chapters.summary: Aftermath: Gerald arrested; the insurance fraud unravels through Rosalind's testimony, implicating her father posthumously. The town's gratitude feels like another kind of payment. Beat: hollow victory; justice without comfort.

chapters.title: Burning the Ledger
chapters.summary: Rosalind decides which secrets deserve survival. She returns the widow's photograph, seals her father's file for the police, and burns her private index of small crimes — keeping only Ada's letters. Beat: release; memory reclaimed as choice, not burden.

chapters.title: When the Letter Burns Again
chapters.summary: Epilogue, mixed POVs. Corin leaves, asking Rosalind to keep Ada's story told; she reopens her office under a new sign: investigations, not filings. On the last page, she lights a candle at the quarry and lets the final copy of the letter burn — because now the town, not paper, remembers. Beat: belonging earned at last.
